titre: Triplett's Social Facilitation, and What It Really Demonstrates
accroche: Forty children turn a fishing reel, alone then in pairs: the founding experiment of social psychology does not prove what it is credited with.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1897, Norman Triplett notices that the best times in road cycling are obtained in direct competition, then with a pacer who sets the rhythm, and only lastly in a time trial, alone. To test the idea in a setting he can control, the Indiana University psychologist sets up fishing reels and has forty children turn the crank as fast as possible. Each one turns alone, then at the same time as a classmate, in an alternating order meant to neutralize practice and fatigue.

## What Triplett Measures

The differences he records are modest, but go in the direction of his hypothesis: in one of the groups, the average goes from 47.48 seconds solo to 41.88 in a pair on the first trial, a gain of 5.6 seconds. For the cycling races he goes through separately, pacer-assisted time trials gain 22.9% in time over unassisted races, and direct competition another 3.5%. Triplett draws an explanation from this: “the bodily presence of another contestant participating simultaneously in the race serves to liberate latent energy.” The study, published in 1898 in the American Journal of Psychology, becomes in textbooks the founding experiment of social psychology.

## What the Statistical Re-reading Finds

In 2005, Michael Strube takes Triplett's raw figures and applies the statistical tests that have become standard since. None of the five comparisons between solo trials and paired trials comes near the threshold of significance. In four cases out of five, performance in pairs is slightly better, but the difference remains too small, and about half the children show no effect at all. In 1898, Triplett had only visual inspection of his curves to judge by; modern statistics does not confirm what he saw in them.

The story does not end there. In 2025, a team rebuilds a setup close to Triplett's reel and runs it with 445 Irish children aged seven to thirteen. The average time falls from 58.4 seconds alone to 55 seconds in the presence of another child, a clear difference (p < 0.001), though more fragile in some subgroups and sensitive to the order of trials. The authors conclude that the effect Triplett announced, on data too thin to show it, exists after all.

## What This Shifts

Nothing in the 1898 data would have withstood a re-reading today. The experiment we tell as founding proved, on its own, almost nothing. What saves it is not its own design, but one hundred twenty-seven years of experiments that ended up finding what it merely announced.

carte.punch: The founding experiment of social psychology proved almost nothing.
carte.idee: In 1898, Triplett has forty children turn a fishing reel, alone then in pairs, and sees in it proof of social facilitation. In 2005, Strube shows that none of his comparisons is statistically significant. In 2025, a replication with 445 children nevertheless finds the effect.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Traces Strube's (2005) critique of the experiment's original data.

quiz.question: What does the story of Triplett's data (1898) show, once re-read with modern statistics and completed by a recent replication?
choix: That the original experiment was already enough to rigorously demonstrate social facilitation
That the 1898 data were too thin to demonstrate the effect, but a 2025 replication finds it
That social facilitation exists only in cyclists, never in children tested in the laboratory
That Strube (2005) definitively invalidated the existence of any social facilitation
quiz.explication: Strube (2005) shows that none of Triplett's five comparisons is statistically significant. A 2025 replication with 445 children, using a setup close to the original, nevertheless finds a clear difference (58.4 s alone versus 55 s in the presence of another, p < 0.001): the effect exists, the founding experiment simply did not demonstrate it.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Before building the fishing reel experiment, what had Triplett observed in racing cyclists?
choix: That direct competition produced better times than racing alone against the clock
That solo cyclists always beat competition records
That the presence of a pacer slowed cyclists through distraction
That times were identical, with or without another rider
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Triplett observes that the best cycling times come from direct competition, then from pacemaking, well ahead of the solo time trial.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In Triplett's table covering twenty children, what is the average time in a pair on the first trial, compared with the time alone?
choix: 58.4 seconds in a pair versus 55 seconds alone, a loss of 3.4 seconds
41.88 seconds in a pair versus 47.48 seconds alone, a gain of 5.6 seconds
22.9 seconds in a pair versus 3.5 seconds alone, a gain of 19.4 seconds
47.48 seconds in a pair versus 41.88 seconds alone, a loss of 5.6 seconds
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Triplett's Table I, covering twenty subjects, gives 47.48 s alone versus 41.88 s in a pair on the first trial, a gain of 5.6 seconds in favor of the pair.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the 2025 replication show, besides finding the social facilitation effect?
choix: That the effect is perfectly stable, identical in all subgroups and whatever the order of trials
That the effect disappears entirely once the sample goes beyond forty children
That the effect is more fragile in some subgroups and sensitive to the order of trials
That the effect appears only in Irish children, nowhere else
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that the difference found in 2025 remains more fragile in some subgroups and sensitive to the order in which the trials are run.
